1. The animation shows a historical buy-versus-rent comparison drawn as a street of houses. A house is "lit" if a buyer was ahead after ten years and "dark" if a renter was ahead. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The label says "illustrative". The focus is "The darkest house", June 2006, where the renter came out $82,385 ahead.

2. Very little changes across the six frames. The title "The darkest house" in frames 1–2 is replaced by the caption "$82,385 behind" in frames 3–6. The house in the center is dark with one small lit door, and it stays labeled June 2006. The rows of houses on either side stay the same. The left side is mostly dark and the right side is mostly lit with warm roofs.

3. The meaning is that whether buying beat renting depended on when you bought. Someone who bought in June 2006, at the peak of the housing bubble, was the worst-off buyer in the dataset. After ten years they were $82,385 behind the renter. The caption reads "$82,385 behind", and the legend defines dark as "renter ahead", so I read the figure as the buyer's shortfall. The lit houses on the right show that many other start dates favored buyers.

4. The animation offers no explicit advice. A viewer might come away thinking that timing and entry price matter a lot, and that buying doesn't automatically beat renting. The footer says "US only · history, not a forecast", which warns against treating the past as a prediction.

5. The advice in 4 is my own reading. The picture and text only state the $82,385 figure and the lit/dark legend. They also say "history, not a forecast", which discourages drawing a prediction from it. They never tell the viewer to rent, to buy, or to wait.
